Reference: Rambachan and Roth (2023)

Model Setting

Researchers who use difference-in-differences (DiD) and event-study designs are often unsure whether the parallel trends assumption holds, and usually assess it by testing for pre-treatment differences in trends (“pre-trends”). Such tests can have low power, and conditioning the analysis on passing them distorts inference (Roth 2022). The paper asks how to proceed instead. Building on Manski and Pepper (2018), it does not require parallel trends to hold exactly. It imposes restrictions on how different the post-treatment violations of parallel trends can be from the pre-trends, formalized as the requirement that the vector of differences in trends δ\deltaδ lies in a set Δ\DeltaΔ chosen by the researcher. Under such a restriction the causal parameter is partially identified, and the paper provides confidence sets that are uniformly valid, in the sense that they account both for statistical uncertainty (the pre-trend is estimated with noise) and for identification uncertainty (even a known pre-trend does not pin down its extrapolation).

Two inference approaches are developed. The first casts the problem as a test of a system of moment inequalities with nuisance parameters that enter linearly, and uses the conditional and hybrid tests of Andrews, Roth and Pakes (cited as forthcoming and abbreviated ARP). These tests control size uniformly, are consistent, and the conditional test has optimal local asymptotic power under a linear independence constraint qualification (LICQ). The second approach uses fixed length confidence intervals (FLCIs), which have near-optimal expected length in finite samples for smoothness restrictions, but can be inconsistent for other restrictions. Simulations calibrated to 12 published papers support the recommendation: the hybrid test for general Δ\DeltaΔ, and FLCIs for the smoothness class ΔSD(M)\Delta^{SD}(M)ΔSD(M). Two applications show how the choice of Δ\DeltaΔ follows from the economic context and how a sensitivity analysis reports the “breakdown value” at which a conclusion ceases to hold. The methods are implemented in the HonestDiD packages for R and Stata.

The target is a linear combination of post-treatment effects, θ:=l′τpost\theta:=l'\tau_{post}θ:=l′τpost​, for a known vector l∈RTˉl\in\mathbb{R}^{\bar{T}}l∈RTˉ: a standard basis vector gives the effect τt\tau_tτt​ of one period, and l=(1/Tˉ,…,1/Tˉ)′l=(1/\bar{T},\dots,1/\bar{T})'l=(1/Tˉ,…,1/Tˉ)′ gives the average effect. Identification comes from the assumption δ∈Δ\delta\in\Deltaδ∈Δ for a researcher-specified set Δ⊆RT‾+Tˉ\Delta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{\underline{T}+\bar{T}}Δ⊆RT​+Tˉ; parallel trends is the special case Δ={δ:δpost=0}\Delta=\{\delta:\delta_{post}=0\}Δ={δ:δpost​=0}. Because δpre=βpre\delta_{pre}=\beta_{pre}δpre​=βpre​ is identified, the restriction limits the possible values of δpost\delta_{post}δpost​ given the pre-trend. The identified set is the set of values of θ\thetaθ consistent with a given β\betaβ:

Choices of Δ\DeltaΔ

The first leading class bounds relative magnitudes. It formalizes the idea that the confounding shocks after treatment are not much larger than those before treatment, which Manski and Pepper (2018) used to calibrate bounds:

ΔRM(Mˉ)={δ:∀t≥0, ∣δt+1−δt∣≤Mˉ⋅max⁡s<0∣δs+1−δs∣}(6)\Delta^{RM}(\bar{M})=\left\{\delta:\forall t\geq0,\ |\delta_{t+1}-\delta_t|\leq\bar{M}\cdot\max_{s<0}|\delta_{s+1}-\delta_s|\right\} \tag{6}ΔRM(Mˉ)={δ:∀t≥0, ∣δt+1​−δt​∣≤Mˉ⋅s<0max​∣δs+1​−δs​∣}(6)

The maximum post-treatment violation of parallel trends between consecutive periods is at most Mˉ≥0\bar{M}\geq0Mˉ≥0 times the maximum pre-treatment violation; Mˉ=1\bar{M}=1Mˉ=1 is a natural benchmark when the numbers of pre-treatment and post-treatment periods are similar. The second leading class imposes smoothness restrictions, suited to confounding secular trends that evolve smoothly:

ΔSD(M):={δ:∣(δt+1−δt)−(δt−δt−1)∣≤M, ∀t}(7)\Delta^{SD}(M):=\left\{\delta:|(\delta_{t+1}-\delta_t)-(\delta_t-\delta_{t-1})|\leq M,\ \forall t\right\} \tag{7}ΔSD(M):={δ:∣(δt+1​−δt​)−(δt​−δt−1​)∣≤M, ∀t}(7)

The parameter M≥0M\geq0M≥0 bounds the change in the slope of δ\deltaδ between consecutive periods, the discrete analogue of a second derivative. With M=0M=0M=0 the difference in trends is exactly linear, which is the assumption behind the common practice of controlling for a group-specific linear trend, δt=γ⋅t\delta_t=\gamma\cdot tδt​=γ⋅t. A combination lets the bound on non-linearity depend on the observed pre-trends:

ΔSDRM(Mˉ)={δ:∀t≥0, ∣(δt+1−δt)−(δt−δt−1)∣≤Mˉ⋅max⁡s<0∣(δs+1−δs)−(δs−δs−1)∣}(8)\Delta^{SDRM}(\bar{M})=\left\{\delta:\forall t\geq0,\ |(\delta_{t+1}-\delta_t)-(\delta_t-\delta_{t-1})|\leq\bar{M}\cdot\max_{s<0}|(\delta_{s+1}-\delta_s)-(\delta_s-\delta_{s-1})|\right\} \tag{8}ΔSDRM(Mˉ)={δ:∀t≥0, ∣(δt+1​−δt​)−(δt​−δt−1​)∣≤Mˉ⋅s<0max​∣(δs+1​−δs​)−(δs​−δs−1​)∣}(8)

Context may also suggest sign and monotonicity restrictions, such as a positive post-treatment bias from a confounding policy, or a pre-existing trend that would have continued:

ΔPB:={δ:δt≥0 ∀t≥0},ΔI:={δ:δt≥δt−1 ∀t},ΔMon:=ΔI∪(−ΔI)(9)\Delta^{PB}:=\{\delta:\delta_t\geq0\ \forall t\geq0\},\qquad\Delta^{I}:=\{\delta:\delta_t\geq\delta_{t-1}\ \forall t\},\qquad\Delta^{Mon}:=\Delta^{I}\cup(-\Delta^{I}) \tag{9}ΔPB:={δ:δt​≥0 ∀t≥0},ΔI:={δ:δt​≥δt−1​ ∀t},ΔMon:=ΔI∪(−ΔI)(9)

These can be intersected with the earlier classes, giving ΔSDPB(M):=ΔSD(M)∩ΔPB\Delta^{SDPB}(M):=\Delta^{SD}(M)\cap\Delta^{PB}ΔSDPB(M):=ΔSD(M)∩ΔPB, ΔSDI(M):=ΔSD(M)∩ΔI\Delta^{SDI}(M):=\Delta^{SD}(M)\cap\Delta^{I}ΔSDI(M):=ΔSD(M)∩ΔI and ΔRMI(Mˉ):=ΔRM(Mˉ)∩ΔI\Delta^{RMI}(\bar{M}):=\Delta^{RM}(\bar{M})\cap\Delta^{I}ΔRMI(Mˉ):=ΔRM(Mˉ)∩ΔI. All of these are special cases of a polyhedral restriction Δ={δ:Aδ≤d}\Delta=\{\delta:A\delta\leq d\}Δ={δ:Aδ≤d} for a known matrix AAA and vector ddd, or finite unions of such sets. The sets ΔSD(M)\Delta^{SD}(M)ΔSD(M) and ΔSDPB(M)\Delta^{SDPB}(M)ΔSDPB(M) are polyhedra. The sets ΔRM(Mˉ)\Delta^{RM}(\bar{M})ΔRM(Mˉ) and ΔSDRM(Mˉ)\Delta^{SDRM}(\bar{M})ΔSDRM(Mˉ) are finite unions of polyhedra, one for each location and sign of the maximum pre-treatment violation; for example Δs,+RM(Mˉ)={δ:∀t≥0, ∣δt+1−δt∣≤Mˉ(δs+1−δs)}\Delta^{RM}_{s,+}(\bar{M})=\{\delta:\forall t\geq0,\ |\delta_{t+1}-\delta_t|\leq\bar{M}(\delta_{s+1}-\delta_s)\}Δs,+RM​(Mˉ)={δ:∀t≥0, ∣δt+1​−δt​∣≤Mˉ(δs+1​−δs​)}. Other polyhedral restrictions, such as one that describes Ashenfelter's dip, fit the same framework.

In the three-period model (T‾=Tˉ=1\underline{T}=\bar{T}=1T​=Tˉ=1, θ=τ1\theta=\tau_1θ=τ1​) the restrictions read ΔRM(Mˉ)={(δ−1,δ1)′:∣δ1∣≤Mˉ∣δ−1∣}\Delta^{RM}(\bar{M})=\{(\delta_{-1},\delta_1)':|\delta_1|\leq\bar{M}|\delta_{-1}|\}ΔRM(Mˉ)={(δ−1​,δ1​)′:∣δ1​∣≤Mˉ∣δ−1​∣} and δ1∈[−δ−1−M,−δ−1+M]\delta_1\in[-\delta_{-1}-M,-\delta_{-1}+M]δ1​∈[−δ−1​−M,−δ−1​+M] for ΔSD(M)\Delta^{SD}(M)ΔSD(M), and the identified set is [β1−bmax,β1−bmin][\beta_1-b^{max},\beta_1-b^{min}][β1​−bmax,β1​−bmin]. Substituting δ−1=β−1\delta_{-1}=\beta_{-1}δ−1​=β−1​ gives:

S(β,ΔRM(Mˉ))=[β1−Mˉ∣β−1∣, β1+Mˉ∣β−1∣]S(β,ΔSD(M))=[β1+β−1−M, β1+β−1+M](10)\begin{aligned} \mathcal{S}(\beta,\Delta^{RM}(\bar{M}))&=\left[\beta_1-\bar{M}|\beta_{-1}|,\ \beta_1+\bar{M}|\beta_{-1}|\right]\\ \mathcal{S}(\beta,\Delta^{SD}(M))&=\left[\beta_1+\beta_{-1}-M,\ \beta_1+\beta_{-1}+M\right] \end{aligned} \tag{10}S(β,ΔRM(Mˉ))S(β,ΔSD(M))​=[β1​−Mˉ∣β−1​∣, β1​+Mˉ∣β−1​∣]=[β1​+β−1​−M, β1​+β−1​+M]​(10)

Under relative magnitudes the set is centred at the naive estimand and its length 2Mˉ∣β−1∣2\bar{M}|\beta_{-1}|2Mˉ∣β−1​∣ grows with the pre-trend. Under smoothness it is centred at the estimate net of the linearly extrapolated pre-trend and its length is always 2M2M2M. This difference in whether the length depends on βpre\beta_{pre}βpre​ drives the later results on FLCIs.

Inferential Goal

The asymptotic normality of β^n\hat{\beta}_nβ^​n​ suggests the finite-sample normal model:

β^n≈dN(β,Σn),Σn=Σ∗/n(11)\hat{\beta}_n\approx_d\mathcal{N}(\beta,\Sigma_n),\qquad\Sigma_n=\Sigma^*/n \tag{11}β^​n​≈d​N(β,Σn​),Σn​=Σ∗/n(11)

The paper constructs confidence sets Cn(β^n,Σn)\mathcal{C}_n(\hat{\beta}_n,\Sigma_n)Cn​(β^​n​,Σn​) that are valid for every θ\thetaθ in the identified set, uniformly over δ∈Δ\delta\in\Deltaδ∈Δ and τ\tauτ, when this approximation holds exactly with Σn\Sigma_nΣn​ known:

Lemma 2.2 handles unions: if Cn,k\mathcal{C}_{n,k}Cn,k​ satisfies the coverage requirement for Δk\Delta_kΔk​, then ⋃k=1KCn,k\bigcup_{k=1}^K\mathcal{C}_{n,k}⋃k=1K​Cn,k​ satisfies it for ⋃k=1KΔk\bigcup_{k=1}^K\Delta_k⋃k=1K​Δk​. It is therefore enough to treat a single polyhedron.

The nuisance parameter has dimension Tˉ−1\bar{T}-1Tˉ−1, which is large in practice (5 of the 12 papers surveyed by Roth (2022) have Tˉ>10\bar{T}>10Tˉ>10), so methods that invert tests over a grid for the full parameter vector are infeasible.

Conditional and Hybrid Tests

The conditional test is based on a profiled statistic, the smallest achievable value of the maximum studentized moment:

η^:=min⁡η,τ~ηs.t. Y~n(θˉ)−X~τ~≤σ~n⋅η(15)\hat{\eta}:=\min_{\eta,\tilde{\tau}}\eta\quad\text{s.t. }\tilde{Y}_n(\bar{\theta})-\tilde{X}\tilde{\tau}\leq\tilde{\sigma}_n\cdot\eta \tag{15}η^​:=η,τ~min​ηs.t. Y~n​(θˉ)−X~τ~≤σ~n​⋅η(15)

where σ~n=diag(Σ~n)\tilde{\sigma}_n=\sqrt{\text{diag}(\tilde{\Sigma}_n)}σ~n​=diag(Σ~n​)​. By linear programming duality, η^\hat{\eta}η^​ equals the value of the dual program:

η^=max⁡γγ′Y~n(θˉ)s.t. γ′X~=0, γ′σ~n=1, γ≥0(16)\hat{\eta}=\max_{\gamma}\gamma'\tilde{Y}_n(\bar{\theta})\quad\text{s.t. }\gamma'\tilde{X}=0,\ \gamma'\tilde{\sigma}_n=1,\ \gamma\geq0 \tag{16}η^​=γmax​γ′Y~n​(θˉ)s.t. γ′X~=0, γ′σ~n​=1, γ≥0(16)

An optimal γ∗\gamma_*γ∗​ is a vector of Lagrange multipliers of the primal program, and the optimum is attained at one of the finitely many vertices V(Σn)V(\Sigma_n)V(Σn​) of the dual feasible set; V^n⊂V(Σn)\hat{V}_n\subset V(\Sigma_n)V^n​⊂V(Σn​) denotes the set of optimal vertices. An example shows the logic. The analogous result holds for the lower bound when LICQ holds in direction −l-l−l. The intuition follows the example above. LICQ makes the bound differentiable in the moment means and makes the Lagrange multipliers at the bound unique, so against local alternatives one dual vertex is optimal with probability approaching one. The non-binding moments are far from binding relative to sampling variation, so the lower truncation point diverges and the conditional test behaves like a one-sided t-test on a single linear combination of the moments, which is the most powerful test of the limiting problem. The result also means that the power of the test is not affected by adding slack moments. Corollary 3.1 follows because the hybrid test rejects whenever the conditional test of size (α−κ)/(1−κ)(\alpha-\kappa)/(1-\kappa)(α−κ)/(1−κ) rejects:

so the hybrid test is near-optimal. LICQ rules out point identification, and the asymptotics describe situations where the identified set is long relative to sampling variation. Suppose Δ\DeltaΔ is convex, α<0.5\alpha<0.5α<0.5, δ∈Δ\delta\in\Deltaδ∈Δ, τpre=0\tau_{pre}=0τpre​=0 and S(δ+τ,Δ)≠R\mathcal{S}(\delta+\tau,\Delta)\neq\mathbb{R}S(δ+τ,Δ)=R. Then (δ,Δ)(\delta,\Delta)(δ,Δ) satisfy Assumption 9 if and only if the optimal FLCI is consistent, meaning that for Σn=Σ∗/n\Sigma_n=\Sigma^*/nΣn​=Σ∗/n:

lim⁡n→∞Pβ^n∼N(δ+τ,Σn)(θout∈Cα,nFLCI(β^n,Σn))=0for all θout∉S(δ+τ,Δ)(30)\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{P}_{\hat{\beta}_n\sim\mathcal{N}(\delta+\tau,\Sigma_n)}\left(\theta^{out}\in\mathcal{C}^{FLCI}_{\alpha,n}(\hat{\beta}_n,\Sigma_n)\right)=0\qquad\text{for all }\theta^{out}\notin\mathcal{S}(\delta+\tau,\Delta) \tag{30}n→∞lim​Pβ^​n​∼N(δ+τ,Σn​)​(θout∈Cα,nFLCI​(β^​n​,Σn​))=0for all θout∈/S(δ+τ,Δ)(30)

The intuition is that a valid FLCI must be at least as long as the longest possible identified set, and its length cannot respond to the data. If the identified set at the true δ\deltaδ is shorter than the maximum, the FLCI is strictly longer than the identified set however small Σn\Sigma_nΣn​ is, and covers fixed points outside it with non-vanishing probability. The conditional and hybrid sets adapt, because their length depends on β^pre\hat{\beta}_{pre}β^​pre​. In the three-period model Assumption 9 holds everywhere for ΔSD(M)\Delta^{SD}(M)ΔSD(M) (length 2M2M2M), holds for ΔSDPB(M)\Delta^{SDPB}(M)ΔSDPB(M) where the sign restrictions do not bind, and holds nowhere for the polyhedra that form ΔRM(Mˉ)\Delta^{RM}(\bar{M})ΔRM(Mˉ).

Simulation Evidence

The simulations use the estimated covariance matrices Σ^\hat{\Sigma}Σ^ of the 12 recently published papers surveyed by Roth (2022). For each paper, coefficients are drawn from N(β,Σ^)\mathcal{N}(\beta,\hat{\Sigma})N(β,Σ^) 1,000 times and nominal 95 percent confidence sets are built for θ=τ1\theta=\tau_1θ=τ1​. Treatment effects are zero, so β=δ\beta=\deltaβ=δ, and δ\deltaδ is either zero (parallel trends) or a “pulse” in which only δ−1\delta_{-1}δ−1​ is non-zero. Performance is measured by the efficiency ratio: an optimal bound on expected excess length among confidence sets with correct coverage (from Armstrong and Kolesar 2018; sharp for convex Δ\DeltaΔ, possibly not sharp for unions) divided by the expected excess length of the procedure. The magnitudes MMM and δ−1\delta_{-1}δ−1​ are expressed in units of σ1\sigma_1σ1​, the standard deviation of β^1\hat{\beta}_1β^​1​, and the median across papers is reported. All procedures control size well.

  • ΔSD(M)\Delta^{SD}(M)ΔSD(M), parallel trends: all procedures have efficiency ratios that approach 1 as M/σ1M/\sigma_1M/σ1​ grows. The FLCI is best for small M/σ1M/\sigma_1M/σ1​, including the point-identified case M=0M=0M=0, where the conditional and hybrid sets have efficiency of only about 50 percent because LICQ fails.

  • ΔSDPB(M)\Delta^{SDPB}(M)ΔSDPB(M), parallel trends: the conditional and hybrid sets are again near-optimal for large M/σ1M/\sigma_1M/σ1​, while the efficiency of the FLCI falls steadily as M/σ1M/\sigma_1M/σ1​ increases, which reflects its inconsistency; the hybrid improves slightly on the conditional for small M/σ1M/\sigma_1M/σ1​.

  • ΔSDRM(Mˉ)\Delta^{SDRM}(\bar{M})ΔSDRM(Mˉ) with Mˉ=1\bar{M}=1Mˉ=1, pulse: the FLCI has infinite length and is omitted; the conditional and hybrid ratios approach 1 as δ−1/σ1\delta_{-1}/\sigma_1δ−1​/σ1​ grows.

  • ΔRM(Mˉ)\Delta^{RM}(\bar{M})ΔRM(Mˉ) with Mˉ=1\bar{M}=1Mˉ=1, pulse: the conditions for optimality fail because the maximum pre-period violation is not unique, yet the ratios approach about 83 percent, so excess length is within 17 percent of the bound.

  • Recommendation: use the hybrid confidence set for general Δ\DeltaΔ, and the optimal FLCI for ΔSD(M)\Delta^{SD}(M)ΔSD(M) or other cases where its consistency and near-optimality are guaranteed. The conditional and hybrid sets perform similarly; the hybrid is preferred on the guidance of ARP.

Sensitivity Analysis and Applications

The recommended practice is to choose a class Δ\DeltaΔ from knowledge of the likely confounds and to report confidence sets for a range of values of Mˉ\bar{M}Mˉ or MMM, together with the breakdown value, the smallest value at which a hypothesis of interest (typically a null effect) can no longer be rejected. For a family Δ(M)\Delta(M)Δ(M) the identification breakdown point is M∗=min⁡MM^*=\min MM∗=minM such that 0∈S(β,Δ(M))0\in\mathcal{S}(\beta,\Delta(M))0∈S(β,Δ(M)), its sample analogue M^∗\hat{M}^*M^∗ is the smallest MMM whose confidence set contains zero, and [M^∗,∞)[\hat{M}^*,\infty)[M^∗,∞) is a valid 1−α1-\alpha1−α confidence interval for M∗M^*M∗. The paper prints the interval as (−∞,M^∗](-\infty,\hat{M}^*](−∞,M^∗]; since zero lies in the confidence set at M∗M^*M∗ with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha1−α, the event with that probability is M^∗≤M∗\hat{M}^*\leq M^*M^∗≤M∗.

The first application is Benzarti and Carloni (2019), who study the cut in the French value-added tax on sit-down restaurants from 19.6 percent to 5.5 percent in July 2009, comparing restaurants with other market-services firms:

Yit=∑s≠2008βs×1[t=s]×Di+ϕi+λt+ϵit(31)Y_{it}=\sum_{s\neq2008}\beta_s\times1[t=s]\times D_i+\phi_i+\lambda_t+\epsilon_{it} \tag{31}Yit​=s=2008∑​βs​×1[t=s]×Di​+ϕi​+λt​+ϵit​(31)

where YitY_{it}Yit​ is the log of before-tax profits of firm iii in year ttt, DiD_iDi​ indicates a restaurant, ϕi\phi_iϕi​ and λt\lambda_tλt​ are firm and year fixed effects, and standard errors are clustered by region. The hypothesis βpre=0\beta_{pre}=0βpre​=0 is rejected (p<0.01p<0.01p<0.01) because of a difference in trends between 2006 and 2007, though the post-treatment coefficients are much larger than any pre-trend coefficient. The concern is industry-specific shocks, which are not smooth, so the analysis uses ΔRM(Mˉ)\Delta^{RM}(\bar{M})ΔRM(Mˉ) with hybrid confidence sets.

  • Effect in 2009: with Mˉ=1\bar{M}=1Mˉ=1 the robust confidence set for τ2009\tau_{2009}τ2009​ is [0.07,0.31][0.07,0.31][0.07,0.31] log points. It is wider than the original OLS interval (roughly 0.16 to 0.23 as read from the paper's figure) but excludes zero. The breakdown value for a null effect is about Mˉ=2\bar{M}=2Mˉ=2: the effect is significant unless post-treatment violations can be twice as large as the largest pre-treatment violation, which matters because 2009 was a recession year.

  • Average effect over the four post-treatment years: with Mˉ=1\bar{M}=1Mˉ=1 the confidence set for τˉpost\bar{\tau}_{post}τˉpost​ includes zero and is about twice as long as for the first-year effect. Bounds on changes between consecutive periods accumulate, so the identified set for the second period is twice as long as for the first.

  • Sources of width: the confidence sets are between 40 and 80 percent longer than the estimated identified set S(β^,Δ)\mathcal{S}(\hat{\beta},\Delta)S(β^​,Δ), so both sampling uncertainty and the length of the identified set matter.

The second application is Lovenheim and Willen (2019), who study state duty-to-bargain laws that require school districts to bargain with teachers' unions, and estimate separately for men and women, with American Community Survey data:

Ysct=∑r=−1121Dscrβr+Xsct′γ+λct+ϕs+ϵsct(32)Y_{sct}=\sum_{r=-11}^{21}D_{scr}\beta_r+X_{sct}'\gamma+\lambda_{ct}+\phi_s+\epsilon_{sct} \tag{32}Ysct​=r=−11∑21​Dscr​βr​+Xsct′​γ+λct​+ϕs​+ϵsct​(32)

where YsctY_{sct}Ysct​ is the average outcome of the cohort born in state sss in year ccc, observed in survey year ttt, DscrD_{scr}Dscr​ indicates that state sss passed a law rrr years before cohort ccc turned 18, XsctX_{sct}Xsct​ are time-varying controls, λct\lambda_{ct}λct​ are cohort-by-survey-year fixed effects and ϕs\phi_sϕs​ are state fixed effects. The outcome is employment and β−2\beta_{-2}β−2​ is normalized to zero, since cohorts at event time −1-1−1 may be partially treated. The stated concern is secular trends that differ with treatment, which evolve smoothly, so the analysis uses ΔSD(M)\Delta^{SD}(M)ΔSD(M) with FLCIs for θ=τ15\theta=\tau_{15}θ=τ15​.

  • Men: pre-period coefficients are close to zero and long-run coefficients are negative. The FLCI at M≈0M\approx0M≈0 is similar to the OLS interval, and the breakdown value for a significant effect is M≈0.01M\approx0.01M≈0.01.

  • Women: the OLS estimate is negative and its interval excludes zero, but there is a downward pre-trend. With M=0M=0M=0, and for all M<0.01M<0.01M<0.01, the robust confidence set contains only positive values, because the estimate for t=15t=15t=15 lies above the linear extrapolation of the pre-trend.

  • Interpretation: imposing the same MMM for both groups yields either significant effects of opposite signs (M<0.01M<0.01M<0.01) or no rejection of a null effect for either (M≥0.01M\geq0.01M≥0.01). Since Chetty, Friedman and Rockoff (2014) find that one standard deviation of teacher value-added raises adult employment by 0.4 percentage points, M=0.01M=0.01M=0.01 allows the slope of the differential trend to change each period by the equivalent of one fortieth of a standard deviation of teacher value-added. Sampling uncertainty is large relative to the identified set when MMM is near zero and less important as MMM increases.

References

  • Rambachan, Ashesh and Jonathan Roth. 2023. “A More Credible Approach to Parallel Trends.” The Review of Economic Studies, 90(5): 2555–2591.

This is the dynamic two-way fixed effects (event-study) regression for the canonical non-staggered design. The outcome YitY_{it}Yit​ of unit iii in period ttt is explained by a unit effect λi\lambda_iλi​, a period effect ϕt\phi_tϕt​ and a full set of interactions between period dummies 1[t=s]1[t=s]1[t=s] and the treatment-group indicator DiD_iDi​. The interaction for s=0s=0s=0, the last period before treatment starts, is omitted, so every βs\beta_sβs​ is measured relative to period 000 and β0=0\beta_0=0β0​=0 by normalization.

Because the regression is saturated in group-by-period cells, on a balanced panel its OLS estimate is a difference-in-differences of sample means:

β^s=(Yˉs1−Yˉs0)−(Yˉ01−Yˉ00)\hat{\beta}_s=(\bar{Y}_{s1}-\bar{Y}_{s0})-(\bar{Y}_{01}-\bar{Y}_{00})β^​s​=(Yˉs1​−Yˉs0​)−(Yˉ01​−Yˉ00​)

The coefficients with s<0s<0s<0 form β^n,pre\hat{\beta}_{n,pre}β^​n,pre​ (placebo comparisons, used to judge pre-trends) and those with s>0s>0s>0 form β^n,post\hat{\beta}_{n,post}β^​n,post​. Identification of βs\beta_sβs​ needs only variation in the group gap across periods; whether βs\beta_sβs​ is causal is a separate question, answered by the decomposition in equation (2) and its primitive version in equation (3). In the three-period example used throughout the note (t=−1,0,1t=-1,0,1t=−1,0,1) there are just two coefficients, β^−1\hat{\beta}_{-1}β^​−1​ and β^1\hat{\beta}_1β^​1​. The whole paper takes the vector β^n\hat{\beta}_nβ^​n​ and its variance as inputs, so nothing later depends on this particular regression: any estimator that is asymptotically normal and satisfies equation (2) can be used.

This is Assumption 1, the only structural assumption on the estimand. It says that the probability limit β\betaβ of the event-study vector is the sum of two unobserved vectors: the treatment effects τ\tauτ that the researcher wants, and the bias δ\deltaδ from differential trends, the path that the gap between treated and comparison groups would have followed without treatment. The restriction τpre=0\tau_{pre}=0τpre​=0 is a no-anticipation condition: treatment has no effect before it starts.

Written by blocks, the decomposition gives

βpre=δpre,βpost=τpost+δpost\beta_{pre}=\delta_{pre},\qquad \beta_{post}=\tau_{post}+\delta_{post}βpre​=δpre​,βpost​=τpost​+δpost​

The first equality shows that the pre-treatment part of δ\deltaδ is identified by the pre-treatment coefficients; this is what makes pre-trends informative. The second shows that τpost\tau_{post}τpost​ and δpost\delta_{post}δpost​ are never separately identified from β\betaβ alone: there are Tˉ\bar{T}Tˉ equations and 2Tˉ2\bar{T}2Tˉ unknowns. Parallel trends closes the system by setting δpost=0\delta_{post}=0δpost​=0. The paper instead links δpost\delta_{post}δpost​ to δpre\delta_{pre}δpre​ through a set Δ\DeltaΔ (equations (6) to (9)), which yields the identified set in equation (4). Nothing in the decomposition is specific to difference-in-differences; any reduced-form parameter that is a causal effect plus a bias whose pre-treatment part is observed fits the framework.

Start from the estimator β^s=(Yˉs1−Yˉs0)−(Yˉ01−Yˉ00)\hat{\beta}_s=(\bar{Y}_{s1}-\bar{Y}_{s0})-(\bar{Y}_{01}-\bar{Y}_{00})β^​s​=(Yˉs1​−Yˉs0​)−(Yˉ01​−Yˉ00​) of equation (1). By the law of large numbers each sample mean converges to the corresponding population mean, so β^s\hat{\beta}_sβ^​s​ is consistent for

βs=E[Yis−Yi0∣Di=1]−E[Yis−Yi0∣Di=0]\beta_s=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{is}-Y_{i0}\mid D_i=1\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{is}-Y_{i0}\mid D_i=0\right]βs​=E[Yis​−Yi0​∣Di​=1]−E[Yis​−Yi0​∣Di​=0]

The identified set collects every value of the target θ=l′τpost\theta=l'\tau_{post}θ=l′τpost​ that cannot be ruled out when β\betaβ is known exactly (no sampling error) and all that is assumed is the decomposition of equation (2) and δ∈Δ\delta\in\Deltaδ∈Δ. A small unstated point: writing max and min, and a closed interval, presumes that the extrema are attained. This holds when the feasible set is bounded or when Δ\DeltaΔ is a polyhedron and the value is finite (a linear program with a finite value has a solution), which covers the cases used in the note. If the bias is unbounded in one direction the corresponding endpoint is infinite, and if the feasible set is empty the identified set is empty.

The relative magnitudes class compares period-to-period changes of the differential trend after treatment with those before treatment. The quantity δt+1−δt\delta_{t+1}-\delta_tδt+1​−δt​ is the amount by which parallel trends fails between periods ttt and t+1t+1t+1, the differential shock of that period. The left-hand side covers the post-treatment changes (t≥0t\geq0t≥0, from the change between periods 000 and 111 onward) and the right-hand side takes the largest pre-treatment change (s<0s<0s<0, up to the change between periods −1-1−1 and 000). Recall δ0=0\delta_0=0δ0​=0, so the last pre-treatment change is δ0−δ−1=−δ−1\delta_0-\delta_{-1}=-\delta_{-1}δ0​−δ−1​=−δ−1​ and the first post-treatment change is δ1\delta_1δ1​.

The scalar Mˉ≥0\bar{M}\geq0Mˉ≥0 is unit-free. With Mˉ=0\bar{M}=0Mˉ=0 all post-treatment changes are zero, so δt=δ0=0\delta_t=\delta_0=0δt​=δ0​=0 for t>0t>0t>0 and the class reduces to parallel trends after treatment. With Mˉ=1\bar{M}=1Mˉ=1 the post-treatment shocks are no larger than the worst one seen before treatment. Since the bound applies to each consecutive change, the level can drift further at longer horizons:

∣δt∣≤t⋅Mˉ⋅max⁡s<0∣δs+1−δs∣for t≥1|\delta_t|\leq t\cdot\bar{M}\cdot\max_{s<0}|\delta_{s+1}-\delta_s|\qquad\text{for }t\geq1∣δt​∣≤t⋅Mˉ⋅s<0max​∣δs+1​−δs​∣for t≥1

which is why identified sets widen with the horizon in the application of equation (31). The class is a cone (scaling δ\deltaδ keeps it inside), so it places no bound on δ\deltaδ when pre-trends are large, and it is not convex because of the maximum on the right-hand side. It is a finite union of polyhedra, one for each location and sign of the largest pre-treatment change, which is how it is handled by the union results after equations (5) and (12). The three-period identified set is derived in equation (10).

The smoothness class bounds the second difference of the differential trend. The term δt+1−δt\delta_{t+1}-\delta_tδt+1​−δt​ is the slope of δ\deltaδ between ttt and t+1t+1t+1 and δt−δt−1\delta_t-\delta_{t-1}δt​−δt−1​ is the slope one period earlier; their difference is the change in slope at ttt, the discrete analogue of a second derivative. The bound holds for every ttt for which the three periods are in the sample, before and after treatment, so the same MMM disciplines the pre-trend and its extrapolation. Unlike Mˉ\bar{M}Mˉ in equation (6), MMM is in the units of the outcome per period squared, so its magnitude must be judged in context (see the calibration after equation (32)).

With M=0M=0M=0 all second differences vanish and δt=γ⋅t\delta_t=\gamma\cdot tδt​=γ⋅t: the bias is a linear trend whose slope is identified from the pre-period, which is the assumption behind adding group-specific linear trends. With M>0M>0M>0 the linear extrapolation is only approximately right. Starting from a known slope, the deviation from the linear path after hhh periods can accumulate to

M⋅(1+2+⋯+h)=M⋅h(h+1)2M\cdot(1+2+\dots+h)=M\cdot\frac{h(h+1)}{2}M⋅(1+2+⋯+h)=M⋅2h(h+1)​

so the identified set grows quadratically with the horizon. The class is a polyhedron, convex and centrosymmetric, and it contains every linear trend. These three properties are what the fixed length intervals of equations (25) to (28) need. In the three-period model the only restriction is at t=0t=0t=0, where it reads ∣δ1+δ−1∣≤M|\delta_1+\delta_{-1}|\leq M∣δ1​+δ−1​∣≤M, that is Aδ≤dA\delta\leq dAδ≤d with rows (1,1)(1,1)(1,1) and (−1,−1)(-1,-1)(−1,−1) of AAA and d=(M,M)′d=(M,M)'d=(M,M)′.

This class combines the two previous ideas: it bounds the post-treatment change in slope, as in equation (7), but the bound is Mˉ\bar{M}Mˉ times the largest change in slope observed before treatment, as in equation (6), instead of a fixed number MMM. The left-hand side ranges over t≥0t\geq0t≥0 (second differences centred at period 000 or later, which involve at least one post-treatment value) and the right-hand side over s<0s<0s<0 (second differences centred at pre-treatment periods, which involve only δpre\delta_{pre}δpre​ and δ0=0\delta_0=0δ0​=0).

It suits a researcher who believes that the differential trend is smooth but has no prior about the level of MMM: the data on pre-treatment non-linearity calibrate the bound. For example, with two pre-treatment periods the only term on the right is at s=−1s=-1s=−1,

Like equation (6), the set is a cone and a finite union of polyhedra, not convex, so the fixed length intervals of equation (26) have infinite length for it, and the conditional or hybrid sets are used.

These three sets encode qualitative knowledge about the direction of the bias. The set ΔPB\Delta^{PB}ΔPB (positive bias) requires δt≥0\delta_t\geq0δt​≥0 in the reference period and afterwards: the confound, for example a simultaneous policy with a known positive effect, pushes the treated group's outcome up, so the event-study coefficient overstates the effect. The set ΔI\Delta^{I}ΔI (increasing) requires the differential trend to rise in every period, before and after treatment, which formalizes the argument that a pre-existing trend would have continued. The set ΔMon\Delta^{Mon}ΔMon allows a monotone trend of either sign; it is a union of two polyhedra, ΔI\Delta^{I}ΔI and its mirror image −ΔI={δ:δt≤δt−1 ∀t}-\Delta^{I}=\{\delta:\delta_t\leq\delta_{t-1}\ \forall t\}−ΔI={δ:δt​≤δt−1​ ∀t}.

This is the working approximation for all the inference results. The central limit theorem gives n(β^n−β)→N(0,Σ∗)\sqrt{n}(\hat{\beta}_n-\beta)\rightarrow\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma^*)n​(β^​n​−β)→N(0,Σ∗); dividing by n\sqrt{n}n​ and treating the limit as exact gives β^n∼N(β,Σn)\hat{\beta}_n\sim\mathcal{N}(\beta,\Sigma_n)β^​n​∼N(β,Σn​) with Σn=Σ∗/n\Sigma_n=\Sigma^*/nΣn​=Σ∗/n. The symbol ≈d\approx_d≈d​ means approximate equality in distribution. In practice Σn\Sigma_nΣn​ is the estimated variance matrix of the event-study coefficients (for example a cluster-robust one), so its diagonal contains the squared standard errors.

The approximation turns the problem into a finite-sample one: a single draw of a normal vector with unknown mean β=δ+τ\beta=\delta+\tauβ=δ+τ and known variance, with the mean restricted by δ∈Δ\delta\in\Deltaδ∈Δ and τpre=0\tau_{pre}=0τpre​=0. This has three uses. First, exact statements become possible, such as the coverage requirement in equation (12), the truncated normal distribution in equation (17) and the expected-length bound in equation (28). Second, linear functions stay normal, for example

Aβ^n−d∼N(Aβ−d, AΣnA′)A\hat{\beta}_n-d\sim\mathcal{N}\left(A\beta-d,\ A\Sigma_nA'\right)Aβ^​n​−d∼N(Aβ−d, AΣn​A′)

which is used for the moments in equation (14). Third, the asymptotic results in equations (19), (20) and (22) show that procedures valid in the normal model remain valid, uniformly over a large class of distributions, when Σn\Sigma_nΣn​ is replaced by a consistent estimate. Letting Σn\Sigma_nΣn​ shrink while Δ\DeltaΔ stays fixed describes large samples in which the identified set is long relative to sampling error.

This is the coverage requirement that defines a valid confidence set in the normal model of equation (11). Reading from the inside: for a given truth (δ,τ)(\delta,\tau)(δ,τ) the data are drawn from N(δ+τ,Σn)\mathcal{N}(\delta+\tau,\Sigma_n)N(δ+τ,Σn​), and the probability is that of the random set Cn\mathcal{C}_nCn​ containing a fixed value θ\thetaθ. The inner infimum is over all θ\thetaθ in the identified set S(δ+τ,Δ)\mathcal{S}(\delta+\tau,\Delta)S(δ+τ,Δ) of equation (4), and the outer infimum is over all admissible truths, with δ∈Δ\delta\in\Deltaδ∈Δ and τpre=0\tau_{pre}=0τpre​=0. The requirement is that even the worst case has probability at least 1−α1-\alpha1−α.

Two features matter. Coverage is for each point of the identified set, not for the whole set at once; since the true θ\thetaθ is one of these points, the true parameter is covered with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha1−α. And coverage is uniform: it holds for every δ∈Δ\delta\in\Deltaδ∈Δ, including values for which the identified set is short or the bounds are not smooth, which is what protects against the distortions of pre-testing. The class of sets that satisfy the requirement is called Iα(Δ,Σn)\mathcal{I}_\alpha(\Delta,\Sigma_n)Iα​(Δ,Σn​) in equations (23) and (28).

The union rule (Lemma 2.2) follows in one line. The null hypothesis is H0:θ=θˉ, δ∈ΔH_0:\theta=\bar{\theta},\ \delta\in\DeltaH0​:θ=θˉ, δ∈Δ with Δ={δ:Aδ≤d}\Delta=\{\delta:A\delta\leq d\}Δ={δ:Aδ≤d}. In the normal model of equation (11) the mean of β^n\hat{\beta}_nβ^​n​ is β=δ+τ\beta=\delta+\tauβ=δ+τ by equation (2), and τ=Lpostτpost\tau=L_{post}\tau_{post}τ=Lpost​τpost​ because τpre=0\tau_{pre}=0τpre​=0. Hence

This is Proposition 3.1: the conditional test (and the hybrid test) has asymptotic size at most α\alphaα, uniformly. The test function ψαC\psi^C_\alphaψαC​ is evaluated at the true value θP\theta_PθP​ of the target under the distribution PPP, with the feasible variance Σ^n/n\hat{\Sigma}_n/nΣ^n​/n in place of Σn\Sigma_nΣn​, so its expectation is the probability of rejecting a true null, that is, of the confidence set missing a point of the identified set. Pointwise results, with the limit taken for each fixed PPP, would not rule out severe size distortions in such cases.

The finite-sample logic is that of equation (17). In the normal model the rejection probability conditional on the optimal vertex and on SnS_nSn​ is at most α\alphaα, and averaging over the conditioning events keeps the bound:

The proposition extends this to non-normal data and an estimated variance under Assumptions 2 to 5 by verifying the conditions of the general result of Andrews, Roth and Pakes; the proof is in the paper's supplement and is not reproduced here. No constraint qualification is used, so the result holds also where the bounds of equation (5) have kinks, for instance with M=0M=0M=0 or when sign and smoothness restrictions bind together. In terms of confidence sets, the statement is the asymptotic version of the coverage requirement of equation (12).

This is Proposition 3.2: the tests are uniformly consistent. The null value tested is θPub+x\theta^{ub}_P+xθPub​+x, a point at a fixed distance x>0x>0x>0 above the upper end of the identified set of equation (5), and the expectation of ψαC\psi^C_\alphaψαC​ is now power. The statement is that the smallest power over the whole class P\mathcal{P}P tends to one, so every fixed point outside the identified set is eventually excluded from the confidence set; the same holds below the lower end. A confidence set with this property shrinks to the identified set, in contrast to the fixed length intervals in the cases where equation (30) fails.

A sketch of why it holds. If θˉ=θPub+x\bar{\theta}=\theta^{ub}_P+xθˉ=θPub​+x then no τ~\tilde{\tau}τ~ satisfies the population inequalities of equation (14), and by the duality of equation (16) applied to the mean vector some dual direction detects this. The bound needs Assumption 8. Convexity and centrosymmetry of Δ\DeltaΔ make the problem one of estimating a linear functional of a normal mean over a symmetric convex set, for which Donoho and Armstrong and Kolesar show that adapting to a favourable truth is nearly impossible. Part (ii) says that the truth is a centre of symmetry of Δ\DeltaΔ; for ΔSD(M)\Delta^{SD}(M)ΔSD(M) this holds at every linear trend, because subtracting a linear trend leaves second differences unchanged. The result is quoted from that literature, not derived in the paper. It does not apply to the classes of equations (6), (8) and (9), where equation (30) shows that the interval can perform badly.

This is Assumption 9, the condition that decides whether the fixed length interval is consistent. The set Δpre\Delta_{pre}Δpre​ is the projection of Δ\DeltaΔ on the pre-treatment coordinates, that is, all pre-trends that are possible under the restriction. The assumption says that at the true pre-trend the identified set is as long as it can ever be, and that this maximal length is finite.

This is the consistency property in Proposition 4.2. The data are drawn from the normal model with variance Σn=Σ∗/n\Sigma_n=\Sigma^*/nΣn​=Σ∗/n, which shrinks to zero, and θout\theta^{out}θout is any fixed point outside the identified set at the truth. Consistency means that the probability that the optimal fixed length interval contains such a point vanishes. The proposition states that, for convex Δ\DeltaΔ and an identified set that is not the whole line, this happens if and only if Assumption 9 (equation (29)) holds.

The mechanism is that the half-length cannot respond to the data. To satisfy equation (12) at every admissible truth, the interval must be at least as long as the longest identified set, so in the limit

If the identified set at the truth is strictly shorter, the interval stays strictly longer than the identified set however small Σn\Sigma_nΣn​ is, and so covers a fixed neighbourhood outside it with probability that does not vanish. If the lengths are equal, the interval converges to the identified set.

This is the event-study specification of Benzarti and Carloni, a special case of equation (1) with calendar years. The outcome YitY_{it}Yit​ is the log of before-tax profits of firm iii in year ttt; DiD_iDi​ equals one for sit-down restaurants and zero for other market-services firms; ϕi\phi_iϕi​ and λt\lambda_tλt​ are firm and year fixed effects; the omitted year 2008 is the last full year before the tax cut of July 2009. Each βs\beta_sβs​ is the gap in log profits between restaurants and the comparison firms in year sss relative to the gap in 2008, so it is approximately a proportional difference. The coefficients for 2004 to 2007 are pre-trends and those for 2009 to 2012 are the four post-treatment coefficients. They are identified by within-firm changes over time compared across the two sectors, and are causal only under parallel trends, which the rejection of βpre=0\beta_{pre}=0βpre​=0 puts in doubt.

The sensitivity analysis applies equation (6) to these coefficients. Its logic can be seen with the identified set for the 2009 effect, which follows from equation (5) in the same way as the first line of equation (10):

[β2009−Mˉmax⁡s<2008∣βs+1−βs∣, β2009+Mˉmax⁡s<2008∣βs+1−βs∣]\left[\beta_{2009}-\bar{M}\max_{s<2008}|\beta_{s+1}-\beta_s|,\ \beta_{2009}+\bar{M}\max_{s<2008}|\beta_{s+1}-\beta_s|\right][β2009​−Mˉs<2008max​∣βs+1​−βs​∣, β2009​+Mˉs<2008max​∣βs+1​−βs​∣]

Reading the paper's coefficient figure, the 2009 estimate is about 0.20 and the largest pre-treatment change (2006 to 2007) is about 0.08, so with Mˉ=1\bar{M}=1Mˉ=1 the estimated set is about [0.12,0.28][0.12,0.28][0.12,0.28]; the hybrid confidence set [0.07,0.31][0.07,0.31][0.07,0.31] is about one half longer, consistent with the 40 to 80 percent reported. The set reaches zero when Mˉ\bar{M}Mˉ is about 2.5, and with sampling error the confidence set first includes zero between Mˉ=1.5\bar{M}=1.5Mˉ=1.5 and Mˉ=2\bar{M}=2Mˉ=2, the breakdown value. These figure readings are approximate; the same figure puts the original OLS interval for 2009 at about 0.16 to 0.23. For the average over four years the changes cumulate, as in the bound shown under equation (6), so the set is wider.

One caution on the breakdown value: the sample breakdown point M^∗\hat{M}^*M^∗ is at most the population one, M∗M^*M∗, with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha1−α, because the confidence set at M∗M^*M∗ contains zero with that probability. The valid one-sided confidence interval for M∗M^*M∗ is therefore [M^∗,∞)[\hat{M}^*,\infty)[M^∗,∞); the interval (−∞,M^∗](-\infty,\hat{M}^*](−∞,M^∗] printed in the paper's footnote has the direction reversed.

This is the event-study specification of Lovenheim and Willen, estimated separately for men and women. The unit of observation is a cell: people born in state sss, in birth cohort ccc, observed in survey year ttt, and YsctY_{sct}Ysct​ is the cell's average outcome (here the employment rate). The indicator DscrD_{scr}Dscr​ equals one if the state passed a duty-to-bargain law rrr years before the cohort turned 18, so rrr measures exposure during school age; the end points r=−11r=-11r=−11 and r=21r=21r=21 collect all earlier and later event times. Negative rrr refers to cohorts that had finished school when the law passed and should be unaffected, so those coefficients are pre-trends. The vector XsctX_{sct}Xsct​ contains time-varying controls with coefficients γ\gammaγ (not the trend slope of equation (7)), λct\lambda_{ct}λct​ are cohort-by-survey-year effects and ϕs\phi_sϕs​ are state effects. Identification comes from differences in the timing of the laws across states. The coefficient β−2\beta_{-2}β−2​ is normalized to zero so that possibly treated cohorts at r=−1r=-1r=−1 are not used as the reference.

in either direction, which for h=17h=17h=17 (counting from r=−2r=-2r=−2 to r=15r=15r=15) is 153M153M153M.
